pr_body:
Ref: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/28083

Right now all database operations are synchronized with a monitor even though it's useless in the vast majority of cases.

The synchronization is only useful when transactional fixtures are enabled.

In production, connections are never shared across threads, as such this extra synchronization is wasteful.

### Motivation

Well, there is obviously the performance overhead of that synchronization.

But beyond this, what prompted me to work on this is that I think it may help with https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/45994. If the lock is only used in test, it's much less of a problem to use a slower lock implementation, which open the door to use a pure ruby monitor that is owned by `Thread` rather than `Fiber`, allowing us to bring back the original behavior.

cc @matthewd @eileencodes, I'd love your thoughts on this.
FYI: @ngan @technicalpickles
pr_comments:
Conditionalizing the lock seems fine to me, and I agree it makes sense if we're switching to a more custom implementation.

The original thinking (which admittedly predates the involvement of the load interlock[^1]) was just that an uncontended lock acquisition would be so close to a no-op that it wasn't worth the branch to avoid it -- I agree it's fine to [potentially] segfault someone who uses a connection they don't have checked out outside of our defined awkward-sharing mechanism.

I suspect this should only apply to `connection`, not additional connections that are manually checked out... and I also have two other, conflicting, thoughts: 1) we probably shouldn't leave the connection in synced mode when it's in the pool; 2) we probably don't need to re-alloc a new lock for every checkout.

[^1]: @jhawthorn and I have discussed the idea of revising and pruning the load interlock now that all loading happens via Zeitwerk/autoloads. When I previously started looking at that, I realised the interlock is still needed to manage _unloading_, but at a glance here, I suspect we might be able to `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor = Monitor`... which if true would at least allow us to avoid mixing that with a new ThreadMonitor[^2]

[^2]: I haven't re-read anything, but off the top of my head, I think we could probably use a mutex if not for `transaction(&)`... and it's arguably already Not Great that we intermix the responsibilities of "don't get transaction states entangled" and "don't both talk to the C API at the same time". Possibly we could/should split those up... though I guess once we've taken it out of any hot paths it doesn't really matter whether we implement a mutex or a monitor.

> an uncontended lock acquisition would be so close to a no-op that it wasn't worth the branch to avoid it 

Yeah, I benched it on my machine. `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor#synchronize` is about `500ns (1.957M (±14.9%) i/s)`, `NullLock#synchronize` about `72ns (13.723M (± 0.3%) i/s)`.

So yeah you'd need to acquire that lock a LOT for it to make much of a difference. I also looked at the implementation, and there is little risks of non-local effects, because MRI's mutexes rely on the GVL so they don't need to use a native mutex under the hood. It's just a bit of book keeping inside the VM.

> 1) we probably shouldn't leave the connection in synced mode when it's in the pool;

Sure. It's easy enough to set `conn.synchronized = false` on checkin.

> 2) we probably don't need to re-alloc a new lock for every checkout.

If it's a test only thing, does it matter that much? Unless the concern is other than performance?
I backported this to our app (Rails 7.0.4, Ruby 2.7.4) and it works great! Thanks for doing this work @casperisfine!

With the backport, in one of our builds (I'm running the build continuously to see if there are any issues), we got a segfault: I'm not sure if it's caused by this change, but I also have never seen this segfault before. Will find some time to investigate this some more but figured I'd post it here to see if this is obvious to anyone.

> With the backport, in one of our builds (I'm running the build continuously to see if there are any issues), we got a segfault:

Hum, I'm not 100% sure, but that segfault suggest you had two thread trying to use the connection concurrently. Normally mysql2 raises an error when this happens, but it might not work 100%, I'll have a quick look at MySQL2.

If you can have this happen again, it would be interesting to add some debug code in there to figure out how this happens.

If I understand this well, it is related to problem I have reported at https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44219#issuecomment-1125524583. I can try to test on our case I had to rewrite meanwhile to not use `Enumerator#next` if welcomed. Would be nice to be able to use `Enumerator#next` again. :pray:

@simi this would fix things in non-test environment since we'd be no longer using `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` in anything but `test` environment. If this lands, the next step would be to swap `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` out with something more custom that relies on Threads (instead of Fibers) for ownership.

> @simi this would fix things in non-test environment since we'd be no longer using `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` in anything but `test` environment. If this lands, the next step would be to swap `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` out with something more custom that relies on Threads (instead of Fibers) for ownership.

My problem was present in all environments (including test). I can disable transactional fixtures for related cases (we're using rspec).
@ngan, did that segfault happen in system tests? Or regular tests?

Merging this as is for now as I can't really see a downside to it, and it opens the door to fix https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/45994 (once we use a different lock for system tests, to be done in a followup).

It is possible that some people out there are incorrectly sharing their DB connections across thread and that it currently semi-work and they may get issues with this change, but I think they should fix their code.

Longer term I think I'd like to get rid of that lock entirely in favor of a `Rack::Lock` in the systems test middleware stack (https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/45994#issuecomment-1304970902), but I had a look at it and it a lot more work, so I'd rather have a solution now than to wait on an hypothetical refactoring.

issue_context.title: LoadInterlockAwareMonitor deadlock when clearing cache (multiple databases, test)
issue_context.body:
With multiple databases, we observe hangs within system tests.

See also https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/371468 (GitLab is at Rails 6.1, Ruby 2.7.5)

### Steps to reproduce
<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

Here's a minimal reproduction with Rails 7.0.3.1

1. Checkout https://gitlab.com/tkuah/multi_database_system_test
2. `bundle install`
3. `bundle exec rails db:migrate`
4. `bundle exec rails test test/system/home_pages_test.rb`

The conditions are:

1. Multiple databases
2. System test where there's an async request which overlaps with the main thread

### Expected behavior

It does not hang, and the test completes

### Actual behavior

It hangs. It looks like it's hanging when clearing query cache (see https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/371468#note_1087203883, and https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/371468#note_1088779499)

A backtrace dump taken while the test is hanging [sigdump-68442.log](https://github.com/rails/rails/files/9539878/sigdump-68442.log)

My suspicion is that:

1. `lock_thread` is true for system tests
3. Therefore both the main thread, and the Puma thread attempt to clear query cache for the same set of connections

So we have two connections:

1. Puma thread takes a `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` lock for primary connection via `Post.transaction`
2. Main thread takes a `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` lock for animal connection via implicit transaction that `create` does
3. Due to 2, main thread attempts to clear query cache for primary connection. **Waits for 1's lock**
4. Due to 1, and because of `lock_thread`, puma thread clears query cache for primary connection. It takes a `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` lock for primary connection which succeds
5. Due to 1, puma thread now attempts clears query cache for animal connection. **Waits for 2's lock**

See [`clear_query_caches_for_current_thread` method](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/e24fbf71fa0a10f63346b9b42604451958740844/activerecord/lib/active_record/connection_handling.rb#L244-L248)



### System configuration
**Rails version**: 7.0.3.1

**Ruby version**: ruby 2.7.5p203 (2021-11-24 revision f69aeb8314) [arm64-darwin21]
comments:
So I dug into this a bit.

Your suspicion is correct about the fact that both the puma and the test threads are blocked on the monitor trying to clear the query cache.

However it makes very little sense, because monitor is supposed to be re-entrant. Since the main thread already hold the lock, it should be able to enter the monitor again to clear the query cache without blocking.

I'll keep digging a bit more, but I must admit I'm quite puzzled about this.

Essentially what we notice is more or less:

```ruby
monitor = ActiveSupport::Concurrency::LoadInterlockAwareMonitor.new
monitor.synchronize do
 Thread.new { monitor.synchronize { p 2} }.join(1)
  monitor.synchronize { p 1 }
end
```

But of course this works as expected. It's very unclear what is special in the reproduction repo so that `monitor.synchronize { p 1 }` blocks.

Oh wow, I tried to add the above snippet in the test case to see if there was anything special, and it does somehow fix the problem:

```
diff --git a/test/system/home_pages_test.rb b/test/system/home_pages_test.rb
index e2466d4..c4c9571 100644
--- a/test/system/home_pages_test.rb
+++ b/test/system/home_pages_test.rb
@@ -6,6 +6,13 @@ class HomePagesTest < ApplicationSystemTestCase
 
     visit 'home_page/index'
 
+    monitor = ActiveSupport::Concurrency::LoadInterlockAwareMonitor.new
+    monitor.synchronize do
+     Thread.new { monitor.synchronize { p 2} }.join(1)
+      monitor.synchronize { p 1 }
+    end
+
+    Thread.current[:deb] = true
     Animal.create!(name: 'cat')
 
     assert_selector "h1", text: "HomePage"
```

This is getting really weird.

From my observations the puma thread was blocked inside `ActiveSupport::Dependencies.interlock.permit_concurrent_loads { super }`, so it seems that having the main thread call `permit_concurrent_loads` unblocks the whole thing. Still no idea why but that's an interesting clue.

One thing that's special about system tests is they need to share the DB thread for the process, otherwise Puma will spin up one thread and Capybara will spin up another and then transactions in tests won't work. I implemented that a long time ago here https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/28083. I suspect any issues with multi-db and system tests are directly related to that "feature".
Or I would check whether parallelization is a component in this as well. Does this occur with PARALLEL_WORKERS set to 1 or 0?

> One thing that's special about system tests is they need to share the DB thread for the process

Yes I'm aware of that. And both threads are stuck calling `clear_query_cache` on the same connection. It should work though, since the main (test) thread already entered the monitor.

> Does this occur with PARALLEL_WORKERS set to 1 or 0?

It's stuck with both.

Ah yep, the two threads are deadlocking because they each hold a (transaction-length) lock of one database, and then try to lock the other. 

It's happening because each thread directly modifies one connection, then attempts to clear _all_ connections' query caches.

Ideally we should only be clearing the query cache for the subset of connections that point to the same physical database or its replicants... but we don't really have a good way of distinguishing that subset.

I had a call with @casperisfine about this issue.

First of all, in the cases it's possible it's best to avoid `Enumerator#{next*,peek*}` as that avoids this issue, but also passing extra state to it, etc.
If the Enumerator is used for e.g. batched queries or DB accesses, a good way is to reimplement those with manual Enumerators/"iterators". For example we can keep the DB cursor, and implement peek/next based on that, and that doesn't involve any Fiber and so just works.
I think this is worth exploring in Rails and might be little code to change, but for that we need to know what Enumerator is typically used for/what APIs would be needed to replace those `Enumerator`s by custom enumerators provided by Rails/AR/DB adapters (with the same methods as Enumerator but not using Fibers).

For the users of Enumerator within a transaction, could you share what you use Enumerator for and some code snippet closer to the actual logic (so it's not a trivial example where there is no need for `Enumerator`)?

If we introduce something like a per-thread monitor (https://bugs.ruby-lang.org/issues/19141), the problem is such a per-thread mutex or monitor would still not let Enumerator-with-Fiber work on a Fiber-based server like Falcon.
So it is an incomplete solution, but it may still be helpful. My current feeling is it's just a workaround, not a real solution.

As @casperisfine mentioned, it'd be nice if we could just remove the lock around the transaction, a lock held so long is likely to cause various problems. And the lock is only necessary for transactional fixtures system tests, which share the transaction and connection across threads (a rather hacky approach which also makes it really hard to reason about it).
Here is a few ideas how to still make transactional fixtures system tests work without the current lock:
* use a global (for all requests) lock on Puma threads. Unfortunately this is not enough with the JS example, as we have the main thread running asserts also accessing the connection. (if we also lock the test/main thread we didn't change anything)
* don't lock the whole transaction but lock only what's necessary around interactions (e.g., socket IO) with the DB. That probably means using asynchronous APIs for the DB, or if there isn't for a DB use a a Thread with a Queue which is the only one actually accessing the connection as a fallback which seems reasonable for system tests.
* are there maybe other mechanisms to efficiently "restore" fixtures after a system test? Maybe some kind of "save & restore" built in the DB which is fast enough? Or maybe for system tests the overhead of the drop + insert fixtures is fast enough or a small enough overhead compared to a system test?

I think the 2nd idea the most promising there, but needs some work in DB adapters, AR, etc.

In any case, using the lock only for the place it's needed (transactional fixtures system tests) in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/46519 seems a good step forward.

```ruby
def synchronize(&block)
  synchronized ? @lock.synchronize(&block) : yield
end

Then call `synchronize` everywhere instead of `@lock.synchronize`

It end up being more or less the same. But right now there is some code doing `adapter.lock.synchronize` we'd need to change it to `adapter.synchronize` which is a bit of a weird interface, especially for something that is optional. So in the end I think I prefer the `NullLock`.
